title: Definition
body_md: A completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) map is called \textbf{number-preserving extendible} (NPE), if it can be extended as written as a convex combination of channels each having the form of Eq.~\eqref{eq:map}.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: A CPTP map $\mathcal{E}$ is NPE if and only if it is a convex combination of CPTP maps, each of which has Kraus operators $\{E_{n,\lambda}\}_{n,\lambda}$ satisfying Eq.~\eqref{Eq:Kraus-operators-NP} for some finite $K$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: For fixed input/output sets $\bm{\mathcal{A}}$ and $\mathcal{B}$, an \textbf{$N$-local quantum} MAC is any channel in which $p(b|a_1\cdots a_N)=\textrm{Tr}\left[\Pi_b(\sigma_{a_1\cdots a_N})\right]$, with $\sigma_{a_1\cdots a_N}$ being a single-particle state encoded by NPE operations.  The collection of all such channels will be denoted as $\mathcal{Q}_{N}(\bm{\mathcal{A}};\mathcal{B})$, or simply $\mathcal{Q}_{N}$ when the input/output sets are clear.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Any channel admitting a decomposition like Eq.~\eqref{Eq:1-N-classical} will be called an \textbf{$N$-local classical MAC}.  For given input/output sets $\bm{\mathcal{A}}$ and $\mathcal{B}$, we denote the family of all such channels by $\mathcal{C}_{N}(\bm{\mathcal{A}};\mathcal{B})$, or simply $\mathcal{C}_{N}$.

title: Remark
body_md: The convexity of $\mathcal{C}_N(\bm{\mathcal{A}};[2])$ is established in Proposition \ref{Prop:binary-out} essentially by absorbing the decoding function $d:\cup_{i=1}^N\mathcal{M}_i\to \{0,1\}$ into the encoding functions $q_i:\mathcal{A}_i\to\mathcal{M}_i$, where $\mathcal{M}_i=\{0,\mathbf{e}_i\}$.  The is possible because $|\mathcal{B}|\leq|\mathcal{M}_i|$ in the binary-output case.  The non-convexity shown in Proposition \ref{Prop:non-convex} follows from the fact that $|\mathcal{B}|=3$ and so $|\mathcal{B}|>|\mathcal{M}_i|$; hence it is not possible to absorb the decoder into the encoders.

label: Prop:N-Local-quantum-I2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Prop:N-Local-quantum-I2}
For $\rho\in\mathcal{H}^{\bm{\mathsf{A}}}_1$ let $\rho_{ij}=\langle \mathbf{e}_i|\rho|\mathbf{e}_j\rangle$.  Then  $I_{2}^{(i,j)}(\rho)=4|\rho_{ij}|$.  Moreover, this value can be attained by parties $i$ and $j$ performing a $\{0,\pi\}$ encoding, i.e. $\mathcal{E}_{a}(X)=\sigma_z^a(X)\sigma_z^a$ for $a\in\{0,1\}$ and $\sigma_z=|0\rangle\langle 0|+e^{i\pi}|1\rangle\langle 1|$.

title: Remark
body_md: The dimension of $(N,K)$-local quantum MAC $\mathcal{Q}_{N,K}$ coincides with the dimension of $(N,2K)$-local classical MACs $\mathcal{C}_{N,2K}$. However, the two sets are distinct, that is, $\mathcal{Q}_{N,K}\ne \mathcal{C}_{N,2K}$ in general. For instance, for $N=3$ and $K=1$, the separation can be directly seen from the quantum violation of fingerprinting inequality in Section \ref{sec:quantum violation}. For the simplest case with $N=2$ and $K=1$ however, this separation is less obvious. We detail a proof for $\mathcal{Q}_{2,1}\ne\mathcal{C}_{2,2}$ in Appendix~\ref{sec:A3 seperation} and conclude it as the following proposition .
